title: The 60-minute setup
intro: One phone, one USB-C stick, no account required. Do these in order. Each step tells you what could go wrong and what finished looks like — not just where to tap.
device: iPhone 15, 256 GB (see step 1 — confirm the real free space). USB-C port is USB 2, up to 480 Mb/s, so a premium stick will not be faster. Buy for reliability, not speed.

steps.title: Measure the real free space
steps.why: Your memory of the phone's storage is not a number. The library does not fit in a plan; it fits in free gigabytes.
do: Read the free-space number at the top and write it in your notes file. That is your budget.
Scroll the app list once. Anything you have not opened in a year is space you can trade for manuals.
Do not delete photos yet. Move them to a computer first — an offline library is not a backup for the rest of your life.
watch: The bar shows categories, not files. Tap a category to see what is actually eating space.
iCloud Photos with 'Optimize iPhone Storage' shows thumbnails, not originals. The originals may not be on the phone at all.
steps.done: You can state your free space in GB without looking it up.

steps.title: Plug the stick in and find it in Files
steps.why: The stick stores. The phone does the reading. If Files cannot see the drive, nothing else in this plan works.
do: Plug the USB-C stick straight into the phone — no adapter if you can avoid one.
Open Files, tap Browse, and look under Locations for the drive's name.
Open it and confirm you can see its folders. Copy one small file in and back out to prove write access.
watch: Nothing appears: try another cable or adapter, unplug and replug, then test the stick on a laptop. Most failures are the adapter, not the phone.
The drive appears but is read-only: it may be formatted NTFS. Reformat to ExFAT, but only after step 3's warning.
A hub or card reader may not pass enough power. Go direct.
steps.done: You have copied a test file onto the stick from the phone and read it back.

steps.title: Format it ExFAT — once, while it is empty
steps.why: ExFAT is readable by Windows, macOS, Linux, cameras and the iPhone. Do this now, before the stick holds anything, because erasing is permanent.
path: press and hold the drive name
do: Confirm the stick is empty or that everything on it is already backed up somewhere else.
Press and hold the drive name in Files, choose Erase, pick ExFAT, confirm.
Eject cleanly by unplugging only after the copy finishes — do not yank it mid-write.
watch: Erasing wipes the stick. There is no undo and no recycle bin on an external drive.
Apple's iPhone guide also lists APFS and MS-DOS (FAT). Do not choose FAT: it caps a single file at 4 GB. Do not choose APFS if a Windows laptop must read it later.
Some cheap sticks lie about capacity. Run a capacity test on a computer before you trust one with the only copy.
steps.done: The drive shows ExFAT in Files' info panel and is empty.

steps.title: Build the folder skeleton
steps.why: A library with no shelves becomes a downloads folder. These five folders make the difference between a pile and a plan.
do: Create 01-manuals — the field manuals and guides.
Create 02-kiwix — offline Wikipedia and other Kiwix ZIM files.
Create 03-recipes — food, water and preservation cards.
Create 04-notes — your inventory, download dates and drill log.
Create 05-apps — installers and README files for phone-side apps.
Mirror the same five folders under On My iPhone so the phone copy matches the stick copy.
watch: Do not nest everything one level deep in a folder called Stuff. You will not find anything under stress.
Names are case-sensitive on some systems. Keep the lowercase-with-dashes convention.
steps.done: Ten folders exist: five on the stick, five on the phone, same names.

steps.title: Send Safari downloads to the phone, not iCloud
steps.why: iCloud can evict a file to save space and leave a cloud placeholder behind. A placeholder is not an offline copy — it is a promise that needs the internet.
do: Set Downloads to On My iPhone and confirm the folder it names.
In Safari, download one small PDF and verify it appears under Files, Browse, On My iPhone, Downloads.
Then copy that PDF into 01-manuals on the phone and onto the stick.
watch: The other choice, iCloud Drive, is fine for convenience and wrong for a survival copy.
Downloads made before this change may still live in iCloud Drive. Move them deliberately.
Some links open a viewer instead of downloading. Use the share sheet and Save to Files.
steps.done: A newly downloaded PDF is physically in On My iPhone, and you have copied it to the stick.

steps.title: Load Tier 0 and Tier 1 from the shelf
steps.why: Start with what you would actually need in the first 72 hours, not with the 6.5 GB encyclopedia.
do: Download every Tier 0 item. These are small cards and one-page references and they take seconds.
Download the two Army survival manuals and the first-aid manual (Tier 1).
Put each file in 01-manuals and rename it so the year is in the name: FM21-76-1992.pdf, not download(3).pdf.
Log each file in 04-notes/inventory.txt: title, source link, date downloaded.
watch: Free to download is not free to reuse. Check the license tag on each shelf card before you repost anything.
If a download stalls, cancel it and retry before switching networks. Half-written PDFs look fine in a list and fail when opened.
Keep the original filename somewhere in your notes. Renaming is fine; losing the source is not.
steps.done: Tier 0 is complete, both Army manuals are in 01-manuals, and every file is listed in inventory.txt with a source link.

steps.title: Open every single file from the stick
steps.why: A file that cannot open is not a library. Test while the internet still works, so a failure is an inconvenience instead of an emergency.
do: Open each PDF from the stick. Scroll to the last page to prove the whole file is there.
Open two that you have not opened before, not the same two favourites.
Fix or re-download anything that fails. Delete broken copies so you do not trust them later.
watch: A PDF that opens instantly usually means Safari cached it. Turn on airplane mode and try again.
Password-protected or DRM files will not be usable offline on another device.
Huge PDFs can be slow to render on a phone. Test the big ones specifically.
steps.done: Every file opens from the stick with airplane mode on.

steps.title: Add Kiwix — but test the small one first
steps.why: Kiwix reads ZIM files: offline Wikipedia, medical references, and whole book collections in one file. It is the highest-value app in the kit.
do: Install Kiwix from the App Store. It is free and needs no account.
Download one small ZIM first — not Wikipedia. Try a single-subject file in the low hundreds of MB.
Open it inside Kiwix with airplane mode on and search for three different terms.
If it works, add the bigger files to 02-kiwix, one at a time, checking free space as you go.
watch: Whether Kiwix on iPhone can read a ZIM straight from an external stick is not confirmed. The project tracker has a 2020 request marked completed and a 2019 failure report. Assume it cannot, keep ZIMs on the phone for now, and test on your own setup.
Wikipedia is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Keeping a copy is fine; republishing it as your own is not.
Sizes change. Check the size on the download page before pulling a multi-gigabyte file over cellular.
steps.done: A ZIM file opens and returns search results with airplane mode on.

steps.title: Make the second copy — one is not a backup
steps.why: Two sticks in two places survive one lost bag, one dead drive and one bad format. One stick survives nothing.
do: Copy the whole library to a second stick. Keep it somewhere else: car, bag, relative's house.
Keep a third copy of the small stuff — Tier 0 and Tier 1 — under On My iPhone, inside the phone itself.
Label both sticks physically with a paint pen: LIBRARY-A, LIBRARY-B, date.
watch: Copying to a second stick is not the same as backing up to the cloud. Both matter; do not confuse them.
Reformatting stick B later will erase it. Check the name before you erase anything.
A stick left in a hot car or a wet bag is a dead stick. Store it dry and cool.
steps.done: Two sticks hold the same library, in two different places, both labelled and dated.

steps.title: Run the blackout drill once
steps.why: The library works only if you have practised using it. A drill finds the weak link while it is still cheap.
do: Turn on airplane mode. Do not just switch networks.
Force-quit Files and Kiwix so nothing is cached in memory.
Open one PDF from the stick, one PDF from On My iPhone, and one Kiwix article.
Look up three things you do not know by heart: a water treatment dose, a canning time and a first-aid step.
Write what failed in 04-notes/drill-log.txt with the date — then fix it.
watch: Being able to open a file is not the same as being able to find an answer inside it. Time yourself.
If the phone is your only light and your only map, a dead battery ends the drill. Carry a power bank and a paper map.
Do not test during a real emergency. Test on a Sunday with tea.
steps.done: You have a dated drill log with zero unresolved failures.

after.title: Then put it down
after.body: A library you check once a quarter beats one you rebuild in a panic. The drill tab has the quarterly routine: check the Army record pages for new editions, re-open every file, refresh the water and food stocks, and copy to the second stick. Nothing in this plan updates itself.
checklist: Every quarter: open every file from both sticks
Every quarter: check the Army record pages for a newer edition
Every year: replace the water in your kit
Every year: re-download the USDA canning guide if it changed
Every year: replace the batteries and test the radio
